headline: Two fixes, one long cleanup
dek: In the 1920s one engineer solved two of the decade's big problems. The world spent most of a century cleaning up after both.

slides.label: What it was meant to do
slides.title: Stop engines knocking and fridges leaking poison
slides.text: Early car engines knocked: the fuel burned unevenly, wore out parts and wasted power. Home refrigerators used ammonia or sulfur dioxide, and a leak could kill the family in the kitchen.
slides.alt: A busy Los Angeles intersection in 1922, with streetcars, early automobiles and a Union Gasoline station
slides.credit: North Broadway and Sunset Boulevard, Los Angeles, 1922. Automobile Club of Southern California. Public domain.

slides.label: What went right
slides.title: Both worked
slides.text: In 1921 Thomas Midgley found that a little tetraethyl lead in gasoline stopped the knock. In 1928 he made chlorofluorocarbons, sold as Freon: no fire, no poison. Cars got more powerful and fridges became safe to own.
slides.alt: A rusted red Atlantic gasoline pump with a yellow and blue Ethyl anti-knock compound emblem
slides.credit: Atlantic Ethyl pump, Leola, Pennsylvania. John Margolies, 1982. Library of Congress. Public domain.

slides.label: What went oops
slides.title: Lead in the air, a hole in the sky
slides.text: The lead came out of tailpipes and settled into the dust of every city, and into children, for half a century. The CFCs drifted up to the stratosphere, where sunlight split them and the chlorine ate the ozone layer.
slides.alt: A NASA satellite map of the globe from below, with a large purple ozone hole covering Antarctica
slides.credit: The ozone hole over Antarctica, October 1, 1998. NASA. Public domain.
also: Workers poisoned making the lead additive in 1924
CFCs are also powerful greenhouse gases

slides.label: What he got right
slides.title: Safe at home
slides.text: The goal behind Freon still holds. The refrigerants that replaced CFCs keep the same promise of no fire and no poison in the kitchen, and are now also kinder to the ozone layer.

slides.label: Could anyone have seen it coming?
slides.title: The lead, yes. The ozone, no.
slides.text: Lead poisoning had been known for centuries, and Midgley was treated for it in 1923. The chemistry that destroys ozone was first described in 1974, thirty years after he died.

portrait.alt: Studio portrait of Thomas Midgley Jr. in round glasses, suit and polka dot tie
portrait.credit: Thomas Midgley Jr. Blank and Stoller, New York. Science History Institute. No known copyright.
